{{Short description|Theorem in statistics}}
In [[statistics]], the '''Lehmann–Scheffé theorem''' provides sufficient conditions for the existence of a best unbiased estimator in a [[statistical model]]. The theorem states that any [[unbiased estimator|unbiased]] [[estimator]] for a quantity that depends on the data only through a [[completeness (statistics)|complete]], [[sufficiency (statistics)|sufficient statistic]] is the unique [[uniformly minimum-variance unbiased estimator]] (UMVUE) of that quantity. The Lehmann–Scheffé theorem is named after [[Erich Leo Lehmann]] and [[Henry Scheffé]], given their two early papers.<ref name=LS1/><ref name=LS2/>

== Introduction ==
Given a vector <math>X= (X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)</math> of random samples from a distribution <math>\mathbb{P}_\theta</math> for some parameter <math>\theta\in\Theta</math>, the goal is to establish [[Necessity and sufficiency|sufficient conditions]] for the existence of an UMVU estimator <math>T^\ast(X) </math> for some quantity <math>g(\theta)</math>, that is, <math>\mathbb{E}_\theta[T^\ast(X)]=g(\theta) </math> and for any [[Bias of an estimator|unbiased]] estimator <math>S(X) </math> it holds

<math display="block">\mathrm{Var}_\theta(T^\ast(X))\leq\mathrm{Var}_\theta(S(X)),\quad \forall\theta\in\Theta. </math>

The [[Rao–Blackwell theorem]] already shows that, given a [[sufficient statistic]] <math>T</math>, the estimator <math>T^\ast(X)=\mathbb E[S(X)\mid T(X)]</math> has a uniformly smaller variance than <math>S(X)</math>, but it does not guarantee that <math>T^\ast</math> is already UMVU. This is where the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem comes in, if <math>T</math> is also [[Completeness (statistics)|complete]], that is, for any real-valued [[measurable function]] <math>\varphi</math> it holds

<math display="block">\mathbb E_\theta[\varphi(T(X))]=0\implies \varphi(T(X))=0 \quad\mathbb P_\theta\text{-a.s.}</math>

==Statement==

As above, let <math>X= (X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)</math> be a vector of random samples from a distribution <math>\mathbb{P}_\theta</math> for some parameter <math>\theta\in\Theta</math> and <math>\Theta</math> an arbitrary set.

Assume that there exists a [[Completeness (statistics)|complete]], [[Sufficient statistic|sufficient]] statistic <math> T </math> for the family of distributions <math>(\mathbb{P}_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}</math>. Then, the following two equivalent statements hold:

* There exists at most one measurable function <math>h</math> such that <math>T^\ast=h(T(X)) </math> is unbiased for <math>g(\theta)</math> and <math>\mathbb{E}_\theta[T^\ast(X)^2]<\infty </math> for all <math>\theta\in\Theta</math>, in which case <math>T^\ast(X) </math> is the unique UMVUE for <math>g(\theta)</math>.<ref name=":0">Lehmann & Casella (1998), p. 87</ref>
* For any unbiased estimator <math>S(X)</math>, if it exists, with <math>\mathbb{E}_\theta[S(X)^2]<\infty</math> for all <math>\theta\in\Theta</math>, the estimator <math>T^\ast(X)=\mathbb{E}_\theta[S(X)\mid T(X)]</math> is the unique UMVUE for <math>g(\theta)</math>.<ref name=":1">Czado & Schmidt (2011), p. 111</ref>
In fact, the theorem does not state that unbiased estimators exist in the first place. However, if they do, then there exists a unique [[Square-integrable function|square-integrable]] UMVUE. Moreover, the estimator <math>T^\ast(X)=\mathbb{E}_\theta[S(X)\mid T(X)]</math> does neither depend on <math>\theta</math>, since <math>T</math> is sufficient, nor on <math>S</math>, since <math>T</math> is also complete.

===Proof===

In the following, the dependence of an estimator on the data <math>X </math> will not be written out explicitly, i.e., we write <math>S</math> instead of <math>S(X)</math>.

First of all, if there is no unbiased estimator for <math>g(\theta)</math>, then there is obviously no UMVUE, and if all unbiased estimator are not square-integrable, then their variances are infinity and the statement is trivial. Thus, we focus on the case where a square-integrable unbiased estimator exists.

''Uniqueness of'' <math>h</math>: Let <math>S=h_1(T) </math> and <math>R=h_2(T) </math> be unbiased estimators of <math>g(\theta)</math> for some measurable functions <math>h_1</math> and <math>h_2</math>. For the expectation of the difference it holds<math display="block">\mathbb{E}_\theta[h_1(T)-h_2(T)]=g(\theta)-g(\theta)=0.</math>Since <math>T</math> is complete, this implies <math>h_1-h_2=0</math>. Thus, <math>T^\ast=h_1(T)=:h(T)</math> is the unique unbiased estimator that is a function of <math>T</math>.<ref name=":0" />

''<math>h(T)</math> is the UMVUE'': Let <math>S</math> be any square-integrable unbiased estimator and <math>S^\ast=\mathbb{E}_\theta[S\mid T]</math>. By the [[Doob–Dynkin lemma|factorization lemma]] there exists measurable function <math>\tilde h</math> such that <math>S^\ast=\tilde h(T)</math> and since <math>S^\ast</math> is unbiased as well, by the above, it must hold <math>S^\ast=\tilde h(T)=h(T)=T^\ast</math>. Thus, by the [[Rao–Blackwell theorem]], it follows<math display="block">\mathrm{Var}_\theta(T^\ast)=\mathrm{Var}_\theta(S^\ast)=\mathrm{Var}_\theta(\mathbb{E}_\theta[S\mid T])\leq \mathrm{Var}_\theta(S), \quad \forall \theta\in\Theta.</math>In other words, <math>T^\ast=h(T)</math> is an UMVUE and according to the first part it is unique.<ref name=":1" />

== Application ==
The Lehmann–Scheffé theorem motivates two general methods to construct UMVU estimators for <math>g(\theta)</math> in models which allow for a complete sufficient statistic <math>T</math>.<ref name=":2">Lehmann & Casella (1998), p. 88–89</ref><ref>Shao (2003), p. 162</ref>

'''Method 1: Determining the function''' '''<math>h</math>'''

The UMVUE, if it exists, is the (unique) solution of the equation<math display="block">\mathbb{E}_\theta[h(T)]=g(\theta)</math>for all <math>\theta\in\Theta</math>. If <math>h</math> is, for example, a linear function, then solving this equation is fairly easy.

'''Method 2: Conditioning on an unbiased estimator'''

First, it suffices to find any unbiased estimator <math>S</math> of <math>g(\theta)</math>, which is often easily feasible. The UMVUE can then be determined by evaluating the condition expectation <math>\mathbb{E}_\theta[S\mid T]</math>. Since the choice of <math>S</math> is arbitrary, it is preferable to choose it such that the conditional expectation is as simple as possible.

== Examples ==

=== Bernoulli distribution ===
Let <math>X_1,\dots,X_n</math> be [[Bernoulli distribution|Bernoulli]]-distributed with probability <math>p\in(0,1)</math>. The joint probability mass function <math>f_p</math> is of the form<math display="block">f_p(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i} = \left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)^{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i} (1-p)^n, \quad x_i\in\{0,1\},</math>thus, by the [[Sufficient statistic#Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem|Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem]], <math>T(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i</math> is a sufficient statistic. It is also complete: Let <math>\varphi</math> be any measurable function such that <math>\mathbb{E}_\theta[\varphi(T(X))]=0</math>. Since <math>T</math> is <math>\mathrm{Ber}(n,p)</math>-distributed, this means<math display="block">0=\mathbb{E}_\theta[\varphi(T(X))]=\sum_{k=0}^n \varphi(k)\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}=(1-p)^n\sum_{k=0}^n \varphi(k)\binom{n}{k} r^k,</math>with <math>r=p/(1-p)</math>. Since the right hand side is a polynomial in <math>r>0</math> that is equal to zero, each coefficient must be zero as well, implying <math>\varphi(k)=0</math> for all <math>k</math>. 

For the estimation of the parameter <math>p</math>, it is now easy to see that the UMVUE is the sample mean<math display="block">\overline{X}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = \frac{1}{n}T(X),</math>since it is unbiased and a function of <math>T(X)</math>. 

Finding the UMVUE for the parameter <math>p(1-p)</math> (that is, the variance of the distribution) is less obvious. According to method 1, we seek a function <math>h</math> such that <math display="block">p(1-p)=\mathbb{E}_p[h(T(X))]=\sum_{k=0}^n h(k)\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}.</math>By defining <math>\rho=p/(1-p)</math>, the above rewrites as<math display="block">\sum_{k=0}^n h(k)\binom{n}{k}\rho^k = \rho(1+\rho)^{n-2} = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{k-1}\rho^k. </math>Comparing the coefficients shows that <math>h(k)=k(n-k)/(n(n-1))</math>, thus, the UMVUE is given by<ref name=":2" /><math display="block">h(T(X))=\frac{n}{n-1}\overline{X}(1-\overline{X}).</math>Noting that in the Bernoulli model <math>X_i=X_i^2</math> and that <math>\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\overline{X})^2 = \sum_{i=1}^nX_i^2 - n\overline{X}^2</math>, the UMVUE is, in fact, the unbiased sample variance <math>S_n^2</math>.

=== Uniform distribution ===
Let <math>X_1,\dots,X_n</math> be uniformly distributed on the interval <math>(0,\theta)</math> for some <math>\theta</math> to be determined. The joint probability mass function <math>f_p</math> is of the form<math display="block">f_p(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\theta}1_{(0,\theta)}(x_i) = \frac{1}{\theta^n} 1_{[0,\infty)}\left(\min_{i=1,\dots,n}x_i\right)1_{(-\infty,\theta]}\left(\max_{i=1,\dots,n}x_i\right), \quad x\in\R^n,</math>thus, by the [[Sufficient statistic#Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem|Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem]], <math>T(x)=\max_{i=1,\dots,n} x_i</math> is a sufficient statistic.

To see the completeness of <math>T</math>, the distribution of <math>T(X)</math> is

<math display="block">\mathbb P_\theta(T(X)\leq t)=\mathbb P_\theta(X_i\leq t, \forall i=1,\dots,n)=\prod_{i=1}^n\mathbb P_\theta(X_i\leq t) = \prod_{i=1}^n\frac{t}{\theta}=\frac{t^n}{\theta^n}.</math>

Thus, for any measurable function <math>\varphi</math> such that <math>\mathbb{E}_\theta[\varphi(T(X))]=0</math> it holds for any <math>\theta>0</math>

<math display="block">0=\mathbb{E}_\theta[\varphi(T(X))]=\int_0^\theta \varphi(x)\frac{n}{\theta^n}x^{n-1}\mathrm{d}x \implies \int_0^\theta \varphi(x)x^{n-1}\mathrm{d}x=0,</math>

and consequently for any <math>b>a>0</math>

<math display="block">\int_a^b\varphi(x)x^{n-1}\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^b\varphi(x)x^{n-1}\mathrm{d}x - \int_0^a\varphi(x)x^{n-1}\mathrm{d}x=0.</math>

This implies that <math>\varphi=0</math> ([[almost everywhere]]) on <math>[0,\infty)</math>. So <math>T</math> is also complete. Its expectation is

<math display="block">\mathbb E_\theta[T(X)]=\int_0^\theta x\frac{n}{\theta^n}x^{n-1}\mathrm{d}x = \frac{n}{\theta^n}\frac{\theta^{n+1}}{n+1}=\frac{n}{n+1}\theta.</math>

Thus, the rescaled estimator

<math display="block">T^\ast(X)=\frac{n+1}{n}T(X)=\frac{n+1}{n}\max_{i=1,\dots,n}X_i</math>

is unbiased and since it is a function of <math>T</math>, it is the UMVUE for <math>\theta</math>.<ref>Lehmann & Casella (1998), p. 89</ref>

=== Exponential distribution ===
Let <math>X_1,\dots,X_n</math> be [[Exponential distribution|exponentially distributed]] with parameter <math>\lambda</math> and suppose the parameter <math>g(\lambda)=\mathbb P_\lambda(X_1>t)</math> should be estimated for some fixed <math>t>0</math>. A straightforward unbiased estimator for <math>g(\lambda)</math> would be <math>\widehat{g(\lambda)}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n 1_{\{X_i>t\}}</math>, however, it turns out to be sub-optimal.

Since the exponential distribution is an [[exponential family]], it is known that its sufficient statistic <math>\overline X=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i</math> is also complete. Moreover, the estimator <math>T=1_{\{X_1>t \}}</math> is unbiased. Thus, according to method 2, the estimator <math>T^\ast = \mathbb E[T\mid \overline X]=\mathbb P(X_1>t\mid\overline X)</math> is the UMVUE. It remains to evaluate the conditional expectation.

First of all, <math>X_1/(n\overline X)\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1,n-1)</math>, which is independent of <math>\lambda</math> (also called [[Ancillary statistic|ancillary]]). In fact, since <math>X_1</math> and <math>S=\sum_{i=2}^n X_i</math> are independent and <math>S\sim \Gamma(n-1,\lambda)</math>, the [[cumulative distribution function]] at <math>y\in(0,1)</math> reads as

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathbb P\left(\frac{X_1}{n\overline X}\leq y\right) &= \mathbb P\left(\frac{X_1}{X_1+S}\leq y\right)\\
&= \int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty 1_{\{x/(x+s)\leq y\}}\lambda e^{-\lambda x} \frac{\lambda^{n-1}}{(n-2)!}s^{n-2}e^{-\lambda s}\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s \\
&= \int_0^1\int_0^\infty 1_{\{u\leq y\}} \frac{\lambda^n}{(n-2)!}r^{n-2}(1-u)^{n-2}e^{-\lambda r}r\mathrm{d}r\mathrm{d}u \\ 
&= \int_0^1 1_{\{u\leq y\}}(1-u)^{n-2}\frac{1}{(n-2)!}\underbrace{\int_0^\infty \lambda^n r^{n-1}e^{-\lambda r}\mathrm{d}r}_{=(n-1)!}\mathrm{d}u \\
&= \int_0^y (n-1)(1-u)^{n-2}\mathrm{d}u,
\end{align}</math>

with the substitution <math>x=ru</math> and <math>s=r(1-u)</math>. Thus, by [[Basu's theorem]], <math>X_1/(n\overline X)</math> and <math>\overline X</math> are independent and the conditional expectation simplifies to

<math display="block">\mathbb P(X_1>t\mid \overline X=x) = \mathbb P\left(\frac{X_1}{n\overline X}>\frac{t}{n\overline X}\mid \overline X=x\right) = \mathbb P\left(\frac{X_1}{n\overline X}>\frac{t}{nx}\right) = \left(1-\frac{t}{nx}\right)^{n-1}.</math>

due to the above derivation.<ref>Shao (2003), p. 163–164</ref>  The constructed estimator

<math display="block">T^\ast=\left(1-\frac{t}{n\overline{X}} \right)^{n-1}</math>

is unbiased and has a smaller variance than the naive estimator <math>\widehat{g(\lambda)}</math> for all possible <math>\lambda>0</math>.

=== Counterexample with incomplete statistics ===
An example of an improvable Rao–Blackwell improvement, when using a minimal sufficient statistic that is '''not complete''', was provided by Galili and Meilijson in 2016.<ref>{{cite journal|title= An Example of an Improvable Rao–Blackwell Improvement, Inefficient Maximum Likelihood Estimator, and Unbiased Generalized Bayes Estimator |author1=Tal Galili |author2=Isaac Meilijson | date = 31 Mar 2016 | journal = The American Statistician | volume = 70 | issue = 1 | pages = 108–113 |doi=10.1080/00031305.2015.1100683| pmc = 4960505 | pmid=27499547}}</ref> Let <math>X_1, \ldots, X_n</math> be a random sample from a scale-uniform distribution <math>X \sim U ( (1-k) \theta, (1+k) \theta),</math> with unknown mean <math>\operatorname{E}[X]=\theta</math> and known design parameter <math>k \in (0,1)</math>. In the search for "best" possible unbiased estimators for <math>\theta</math>, it is natural to consider <math>X_1</math> as an initial (crude) unbiased estimator for <math>\theta</math> and then try to improve it. Since <math>X_1</math> is not a function of <math>T = \left( X_{(1)}, X_{(n)}  \right)</math>, the minimal sufficient statistic for <math>\theta</math> (where <math>X_{(1)} = \min_i X_i </math> and <math>X_{(n)} = \max_i X_i </math>), it may be improved using the Rao–Blackwell theorem as follows: 

:<math>\hat{\theta}_{RB} =\operatorname{E}_\theta[X_1\mid X_{(1)}, X_{( n)}] = \frac{X_{(1)}+X_{(n)}} 2.</math>

However, the following unbiased estimator can be shown to have lower variance: 

:<math>\hat{\theta}_{LV} = \frac 1 {k^2\frac{n-1}{n+1}+1} \cdot \frac{(1-k)X_{(1)} + (1+k) X_{(n)}} 2.</math> 

And in fact, it could be even further improved when using the following estimator:  

:<math>\hat{\theta}_\text{BAYES}=\frac{n+1} n \left[1- \frac{\frac{X_{(1)} (1+k)}{X_{(n)} (1-k)}-1}{ \left (\frac{X_{(1)} (1+k)}{X_{(n)} (1-k)}\right )^{n+1} -1} \right] \frac{X_{(n)}}{1+k}</math>

The model is a [[Scale parameter|scale model]]. Optimal [[Equivariant Estimator|equivariant estimators]] can then be derived for [[loss function]]s that are invariant.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Taraldsen|first=Gunnar|date=2020|title=Micha Mandel (2020), "The Scaled Uniform Model Revisited," The American Statistician, 74:1, 98–100: Comment|url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2020.1769727|journal=The American Statistician|volume=74|issue=3|pages=315|doi=10.1080/00031305.2020.1769727|s2cid=219493070 |issn=|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
